issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
*Request for comment.*

> **TL;DR.** OPD needs a teacher model that returns per-token logprob targets in the training inner
> loop. The deciding factor is **how many logprobs per token** we need: our stack (MarinSkyRL) today
> does **top-K sparse forward-KL** (default **K=256**), *not* the full-vocab reverse-KL of the
> DeepSeek-V4 recipe. Top-K payloads are small and travel cheaply over a network; **full-vocab is
> ~300 KB/token → GB/step and is only tractable co-located.** That single fact reorders the options.
>
> **My lean: Option 3 (permanent marin-serve teacher endpoints on CoreWeave, top-K), plus Option 4
> (forward-only co-located teacher) reserved as a "full-vocab fast-track" if an ablation ever shows
> we need it.** Option 3 reuses the remote teacher-client MarinSkyRL already has, decouples serving
> optimization from the RL loop, and amortizes across OPD + judge + eval. Options 1 and 2 are
> prototyping and single-hero-run tools, respectively. **Tell me where this is wrong** — especially
> on (a) whether K≤20 provider ceilings are disqualifying, (b) whether full-vocab reverse-KL is worth
> building for at all, and (c) whether the forward-only teacher (Option 4) should be the default
> instead of Option 3.

## Context

On-policy distillation (OPD) is load-bearing in our post-training plan: the distillation stage
distills RL-trained experts into the student via OPD, *if* we have teacher-logit infra — otherwise we
fall back to the weaker off-policy SFT-distill path. The [#7074](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7074)
cost analysis sizes the pipeline as **RL K experts → OPD into the student** (Nemotron-style path),
where the OPD leg is student-rollout-dominated and roughly RL-scale in cost.

**Why this decision matters NOW:** OPD is a complex, jointly-optimized system — the teacher serving
path is tightly coupled to the training loop (the teacher is queried in the inner loop, per batch of
student-generated tokens). Getting it working reliably is hard, and once it works there is a strong
incentive to never touch the plumbing again. That makes the early architectural choices effectively
*sticky*. This RFC aims to make that choice a deliberate one, with eyes open about what each option
forecloses.

The core question: **how do we serve the teacher model that provides logprob targets during OPD?**

---

## The logprobs crux (the deciding technical factor)

OPD's distillation loss is a per-token KL between the student and teacher distributions over the
generated positions. The teacher must return a **probability distribution over tokens** at each
position — not a generated sequence or a reward score. *How much* of that distribution we need is the
crux, and it splits cleanly into two regimes:

- **Top-K (what our stack does today).** MarinSkyRL's `distillation_trainer.py` requests
  `cfg.teacher.top_k_logprobs` (default **K=256**, `config/ppo_base_config.yaml`), carries a
  `teacher_top_k_logprobs: [batch, seq, K]` tensor (`training_batch.py`), and computes the loss with
  `forward_kl_from_sparse` (`utils/distillation_utils.py`) — a **forward**-KL over the teacher's
  top-K support (`kl = Σ_k teacher_p·(teacher_logp − student_logp_at_k)`). A remote
  `TeacherInferenceEngineClient.score_sequences` (with student↔teacher retokenization) already exists.
  **Top-K logprobs are a small payload** (K values + K indices per token) and travel cheaply over a
  network — so top-K OPD is *not* gated by where the teacher lives.
- **Full-vocab (the DeepSeek-V4 aspiration).** V4's OPD is full-vocabulary **reverse**-KL
  (`L = Σᵢ wᵢ·D_KL(π_θ ∥ π_Eᵢ)`, trajectories sampled from the student). This is a **different loss in
  both support (full vs top-K) and direction (reverse vs forward)** from what MarinSkyRL implements
  today. It is strictly richer — but per the bandwidth wrinkle below, it is only tractable with a
  **co-located** teacher.

**The bandwidth wrinkle (why top-K is the practical default, and why providers only offer top-k).**
A full-vocab logprob vector is ~vocab (≈128–150k) × 2 bytes ≈ **~300 KB per generated token**. Across
an OPD inner-loop batch that is **on the order of GB/step moving over the network, every step** — WAN
is prohibitive, intra-DC is heavy, and only a co-located teacher on the same NCCL/IPC fabric makes it
free. This is almost certainly *why* hosted providers expose only top-k logprobs (OpenAI: top-20): the
full distribution is too expensive to serialize per token. **Consequence:** any *networked* teacher —
a provider (Option 1) or a permanently hosted endpoint (Option 3) — is effectively **top-K only**.
Full-vocab reverse-KL is available only to a **co-located** teacher (Option 2's in-cluster engines, or
Option 4's forward-only teacher). If we want full-vocab, we want an **OPD fast-track for co-located
jobs** alongside whatever we run for the common case.

**Working assumption for this RFC:** unless an ablation shows full-vocab reverse-KL is worth its cost,
we should **plan for top-K** (start at the K our stack already defaults to, and treat provider K≤20 as
the one hard ceiling to check). Full-vocab is then an opt-in co-located path, not the baseline that
gates the whole serving decision. *(We found no published "safe K" ablation in our notes — see Q1.)*

---

## Option 1 — serve the teacher from a cloud inference provider (Together / Fireworks / OpenAI)

The teacher is a hosted model behind an API. The OPD trainer calls the provider's completions/chat
endpoint with `logprobs` to get per-token distributions.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Least new plumbing** — no serving infra to build or maintain; one less component to jointly optimize for throughput. | **Provider top-k ceiling vs. our K.** Providers cap logprobs low (OpenAI: top-20). Our stack defaults to **K=256**; whether K≤20 is adequate is an open ablation (Q1). Full-vocab reverse-KL is off the table on any provider. **This is the gating question for this option.** |
| **Maximum teacher flexibility** — swap teachers by changing a model name; no weight staging. | **Teacher availability is not in our control.** A provider can deprecate/drop a model mid-campaign; teacher selection follows their catalog, not our research needs. |
| **Fast to prototype** — an API key unblocks OPD-loop development today. | **No path to custom Marin teachers** — distilling from a Marin-trained checkpoint (the point of expert iteration) needs a separate deal / custom serving. |
| **Elastic capacity** — no fixed GPU commitment; pay per token. | **Per-token cost + throughput risk at scale.** OPD processes ~10⁹–10¹⁰ training tokens (#7074); provider pricing is expensive at that volume, and **rate-limit / tail-latency variance is an inner-loop hazard** — a single slow or throttled teacher call stalls the whole synchronous train step, not just a batch's cost. |
| | **Redundancy requires N integrations.** Each provider has a different API surface, logprob format, and rate-limit regime. Multi-provider fallback is real integration work, not a config flip. |
| | **Reproducibility risk** — providers may silently update served weights, breaking experiment reproducibility. |

---

## Option 2 — co-host the teacher with the student in a single large allocation

The teacher, student, and reference model all live in one Ray cluster / GPU allocation. The
teacher is a set of vLLM inference engines scheduled alongside the training actors. This is the
"everything in one Slurm job" model.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Infra already partially built** — MarinSkyRL already co-hosts policy + inference engines in one Ray cluster; the teacher is "one more served model," and the remote teacher-client already exists. | **The FLOP-utilization dance.** OPD is a 3-stage pipeline: student generates → teacher scores → student trains. When the student generates, the teacher is idle; when the teacher scores, the student is idle. Balancing all three at high utilization must be re-tuned per model size / batch / pipeline change. (SkyRL's `fully_async` 2-stage pipeline is already hard to balance; a 3rd stage compounds it.) |
| **Full control of quantization + weights** — quantized teachers, custom architectures, Marin-trained checkpoints all work. | **Resource-intensive** — a 120B-class teacher + student + reference in one allocation is a large footprint per experiment → **fewer concurrent experiments**. Trades experiment parallelism for self-contained runs. |
| **Low-latency hop** — teacher scoring is on the same Ray fabric as rollout, so batching is tight. | **Still top-K if the teacher is a vLLM engine** — vLLM's API returns top-K, not the full logits tensor (see Option 3 caveat). Full-vocab here needs a custom serving hook, i.e. it collapses into Option 4. |
| **Bugs are patchable** — full source access; no provider dependency. | **Infra burden** — one more thing the RL-launcher/SkyRL stack must schedule, configure, and debug. |

---

## Option 3 — permanently hosted teachers via marin-serve on dedicated CoreWeave compute

A set of CoreWeave GPUs is dedicated to long-running teacher endpoints (marin-serve / vLLM), queried
over the network by any consumer — OPD trainers, LLM judges, coding agents, eval pipelines, vibe
tests. The teacher is "always warm." **Top-K by nature of the network hop** (per the bandwidth crux).

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Decoupled optimization** — the serving pipeline (continuous batching, prefix caching, quantization, KV-cache tuning) is optimized **independently** of the RL/OPD run. No joint-scheduling dance. | **Top-K only.** The network hop caps us at top-K logprobs (bandwidth crux) — fine for our current top-K forward-KL loss, but forecloses full-vocab reverse-KL. If the endpoint's K is enough (Q1), a non-issue; if we later want full-vocab, this option can't provide it (use Option 4). |
| **No top-*20* ceiling** — we run the model, so we set K (e.g. 256, matching our default) rather than being stuck at a provider's ~20. | **Resource-intensive** — dedicates GPUs full-time to hosting, removing them from the experiment pool. Trades raw training throughput for serving readiness. |
| **Multi-purpose amortization** — one hosted teacher serves OPD + the LLM-judge tier + coding agents + eval + vibe tests. The post-training plan already asks for "~10 hosted endpoints we can update quickly" — this *is* that infra, and concurrent OPD runs share it. | **High infra burden + single point of failure** — we own uptime, autoscaling, model-swapping, failure recovery. If the endpoint goes down, all dependent OPD runs stall. |
| **Marin-trained teachers work natively** — swap the hosted checkpoint; no provider deal, no API integration. Future-proof for expert-iteration. | **Forces teacher prioritization** — dedicated GPUs can't host every teacher at once; we commit to a small primary set, limiting experiment diversity. |
| **Faster wall-clock than Option 2** — continuous batching across all consumers + prefix caching means the teacher runs at high utilization *without* the pipeline-imbalance tax. | **Network latency** — same-region intra-DC RTT is sub-millisecond (negligible vs. WAN), but it is still a hop; per-batch latency is nonzero. |
| **Reuses existing plumbing** — MarinSkyRL's `TeacherInferenceEngineClient` already targets a remote scoring engine and returns top-K; Option 3 is the closest to what's built. Also exercises marin-serve / the Inference Server ([#6500](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/6500)) under real load. | |

---

## Option 4 — frozen, forward-only teacher co-resident in the trainer

A distinct implementation of "co-located": the teacher is a **frozen, forward-only** module in the
**training framework itself** (FSDP/Megatron forward pass, no generation engine), with the teacher
logits fed **straight into the loss**. This is a common OPD/KD setup and the only option that cleanly
supports **full-vocab reverse-KL**.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Full-vocab by construction, no serialization hop** — logits never leave the training mesh, so the ~300 KB/token bandwidth wall (and vLLM's top-K API limit) simply don't apply. The natural home for full-vocab reverse-KL. | **Teacher lives in the training allocation** — teacher weights occupy HBM in the same job; a 120B teacher + student + ref is a large single footprint (same experiment-parallelism cost as Option 2). |
| **No generation-serving stack to schedule** — no vLLM engine, no continuous-batching tuning, no separate endpoint. Just a forward pass, sharded like any frozen model. | **Teacher forward contends with training compute** on the same mesh; the forward FLOPs are inline with the step (though there's no idle-teacher pipeline-imbalance tax — the forward is a synchronous part of the loss). |
| **Simplest correctness story** — no cross-process logprob transport, no top-K renormalization approximation, no retokenization mismatch; teacher and student share the trainer's tokenizer/dtype. | **Least flexible swapping** — changing teachers means re-staging weights into the training job, not hitting a different endpoint. |
| **Exact reverse-KL** — student-sampled trajectories + full teacher distribution is precisely the V4 recipe. | **Not multi-purpose** — this teacher serves only the OPD loss and only for the run's duration; the "~10 hosted endpoints" need is unmet by this option (that's Option 3). |

---

## Cross-cutting considerations

### The teacher-oracle abstraction (delaying lock-in)

The core concern — early lock-in because OPD is hard to get working — applies to all four options. One
structural mitigation: **architect the OPD trainer against a generic `TeacherLogprobOracle` interface**
— given a batch of student-generated token sequences, return the teacher's logprob targets at each
position. The four options become four *backends* (API client, co-hosted vLLM, remote marin-serve
endpoint, in-trainer forward-only teacher). MarinSkyRL's `TeacherInferenceEngineClient` is already
close to this boundary.

This makes the serving decision **reversible** for the *networked, top-K* backends (Options 1, 2-vLLM,
3 are interchangeable behind the interface). **The one seam the interface cannot paper over is top-K
vs full-vocab:** a full-vocab reverse-KL loss (Option 4) changes the loss's shape and the data the
oracle returns, so it is not a drop-in backend swap — it's a second loss path. Decide the
top-K-vs-full-vocab question first (Q1); *within* top-K, the backend is a swap.

### Quantization parity

For RL scoring, a quantized teacher (FP8/AWQ) is fine — the reward signal tolerates small logprob
perturbation. For **distillation**, the teacher's logprobs ARE the target, and quantization is a
systematic perturbation that compounds token-by-token. Options 2/3/4 give full control over teacher
quantization (and the ability to validate parity against an unquantized reference); Option 1's
quantization is whatever the provider serves. Whether it matters depends on teacher size and the loss's
error tolerance.

### The small-model distillation angle

The plan also ships smaller sizes via strong-to-weak distillation **from the flagship**. This is a
*different* OPD use case (flagship → small model, not expert → student) but reuses the same teacher
serving infra, and it is long-context / high-throughput / high-value. Whichever option we pick should
handle both.

---

## Open questions for discussion

1. **What K is safe? (the pivotal question)** Our stack defaults to **K=256** top-K forward-KL. Is
   K≤20 (provider ceiling, Option 1) adequate, or do we need K≈256 (self-hosted, Options 2/3), or true
   full-vocab reverse-KL (Option 4)? We found **no published safe-K ablation** in our notes — this
   likely needs a quick internal ablation, and its answer determines which options are even eligible.

2. **Is full-vocab reverse-KL worth building?** It's the DeepSeek-V4 recipe and strictly richer, but
   it's co-located-only (bandwidth) and a second loss path (not just a backend swap). If K=256 top-K
   forward-KL is "good enough," we can drop full-vocab entirely and the serving decision simplifies to
   Options 1/3. If not, Option 4 becomes load-bearing.

3. **Teacher size envelope:** What is the largest teacher we plan to distill from? A 120B-class teacher
   makes the co-located options (2/4) expensive (the allocation balloons) and pushes the common case
   toward Option 3. A ≤70B teacher is more tractable everywhere.

4. **Concurrency:** How many OPD experiments run simultaneously? "Many, sharing one teacher" → Option
   3's amortization dominates. "One at a time" → Option 2/4's self-contained simplicity is fine.

5. **Marin-trained teacher timeline:** When do we first need to distill from a Marin-trained checkpoint
   (not a third-party model)? That's the hard deadline by which Option 1 must be replaced by 2/3/4.

6. **Is a hybrid viable?** Option 3 (primary/production, top-K) + Option 1 as elastic overflow + Option
   4 as a full-vocab fast-track for the one hero run that needs it. The oracle abstraction makes the
   top-K backends interchangeable; Option 4 is the deliberate exception.

---

## Suggested framing for a decision

Rather than committing to one option now, a **phased path** that hedges lock-in:

1. **Phase 0 (fast):** Settle Q1 with a small **K ablation** (top-20 vs top-256 vs full-vocab on a
   representative teacher/student) — this is the decision that gates everything. In parallel, harden the
   `TeacherLogprobOracle` boundary around MarinSkyRL's existing top-K teacher-client, and validate the
   OPD loop end-to-end against **Option 1** (API, top-20) for loop correctness — the loop, not the
   backend, is the hard part.
2. **Phase 1:** Stand up a dedicated **marin-serve teacher endpoint (Option 3, top-K, K≈256)** for the
   primary production teacher; point the oracle at it. This is also the LLM-judge + eval endpoint the
   plan already needs, so the infra investment is shared, not OPD-specific.
3. **Phase 2 (conditional):** If — and only if — the Phase-0 ablation shows full-vocab reverse-KL is
   worth it, build **Option 4** (forward-only co-located teacher) as the full-vocab fast-track for the
   runs that need it. **Option 2** (co-hosted vLLM) is worth it only for a single large hero run where
   even Option 3's intra-DC hop is intolerable and full-vocab isn't required.

The interface boundary means the *top-K* backends are swaps, not redesigns. The genuinely sticky
decisions are the two the ablation forces: **top-K-vs-full-vocab** and **forward-vs-reverse KL**.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
Decisions here seem reasonable to me. Our experience so far has been that for trained models, the logprobs drop extremely quickly off of the top-few, so top-K feels pretty safe? Not sure the best way to validate that e.g. top-20/256/whatever wouldn't drop too much on the floor. I feel building things around the `TeacherLogprobOracle` interface is the right call - we can either present this via the OpenAI API against an inference provider or our own internal models, with little switching cost.

For running our own long-term inference endpoints, my concern would be two-fold: 

(a) yes, the maintainence burden, but that should be manageable, since we can run multiple instances and setup the clients to be failure tolerant. 
(b) GPUs are precious and we can't use the idled GPUs if they aren't being actively used by a trainer


For (b) if the server bringup is coupled to the data-gen/training process, I'm less concerned.

issues.author: ihodes
issues.body:
## Goal

Select and implement a pinned, open, text-only validation suite that approximates the capabilities in the current Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index across Marin pretraining, mid-training, and post-training checkpoints.

This is the concrete successor to #6050 and the eval-selection workstream under #6503. It is a **generative validation suite for both base/pretraining and post-trained checkpoints**, complementary to the lightweight PPL competency proxies in #5819. Benchmark items must remain isolated from training data, while results should be available alongside regular pretraining validation dashboards.

The suite is a proxy, not a reproduction of Artificial Analysis: several AA datasets and grading harnesses are private, and agentic behavior cannot be faithfully reduced to text-only tasks.

## Proposed benchmark mapping

| AA benchmark | Open text-only replacement | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **GDPval-AA v2** | **FinanceBench + IFBench + DS-1000** | Composite proxy for professional analysis, constraint-following, and practical technical work. There is no good single text-only equivalent for GDPval's agentic knowledge work and file outputs. |
| **τ³-Banking** | **τ²-Bench-Verified Retail** | Closest match for stateful customer-service workflows, policy adherence, and tool use. Use **BFCL** only as an easier, weaker fallback. |
| **Terminal-Bench v2.1** | **OT-TBench-Lite** | Direct lightweight terminal-agent proxy. |
| **SciCode** | **DS-1000 + CruxEval** | DS-1000 covers practical scientific/data coding; CruxEval adds code-execution reasoning. |
| **Humanity's Last Exam** | **MMLU-Pro + OlympiadBench Math** | MMLU-Pro supplies broad coverage; OlympiadBench supplies the hard tail. |
| **GPQA Diamond** | **MMLU-Pro science subset** | Easy to run but weaker than GPQA. Retaining open **GPQA Diamond** itself is the more faithful option if contamination policy permits. |
| **CritPt** | **OlympiadBench Physics** | Best simple open physics proxy, though exam-level rather than research-level. |
| **AA-Omniscience** | **Open factual QA with abstention and negative marking** | Use a SimpleQA-style or TriviaQA-derived held-out set; score correct `+1`, abstain `0`, incorrect `−1`. Report accuracy and hallucination rate separately as well as the signed score. |
| **AA-LCR** | **MRCR** | Good open long-context proxy, though more retrieval-oriented than AA-LCR's document synthesis. Cover the intended 10K–100K-token range. |

Artificial Analysis methodology: https://artificialanalysis.ai/methodology/intelligence-benchmarking

## Scoring proposal

- Preserve the current AA component weights so the proxy has a stable composite: GDPval proxy 20%, τ³ proxy 14%, Terminal proxy 16%, SciCode proxy 8%, HLE proxy 12%, GPQA proxy 6%, CritPt proxy 6%, Omniscience proxy 12%, and LCR proxy 6%.
- For composite replacements, normalize each constituent metric and macro-average within the component before applying the component weight.
- Publish every component score alongside the aggregate. Call the aggregate **Marin AA-II proxy**, never an AA score.
- Treat the weights and task revisions as a versioned configuration so the suite remains reproducible when AA or upstream benchmarks change.

## Definition of done

- [ ] Confirm dataset availability, licenses, canonical splits, and exact benchmark variants; pin dataset and harness revisions.
- [ ] Add explicit eval-only manifests and contamination metadata. No benchmark test item may enter training or core PPL tracking, consistent with #5819.
- [ ] Implement each component behind Marin's standard OpenAI-compatible eval entrypoint and make the suite selectable by one versioned config in #6503.
- [ ] Pin prompts/chat templates, decoding parameters, parsers/graders, seeds, repeats, tokenizer/model revisions, and context lengths.
- [ ] Emit raw per-item outputs plus component metrics, confidence intervals, runtime/cost, failure counts, and the versioned composite score.
- [ ] Provide a tiny deterministic smoke subset for scheduled regression testing, plus the full-suite path.
- [ ] Run a representative model panel and measure repeatability and rank correlation against available AA/Harbor component results. Document where the text-only proxy fails to preserve rankings.
- [ ] Publish results through the eval results/leaderboard path tracked by #6043 and #6503.
- [ ] Document how to add, replace, or retire a component without silently changing historical scores.

## Related work

- #6050 — original AA-II eval TBD (closed in favor of July work)
- #6503 — automated eval system parent Epic
- #6863 — July Evalchemy/Harbor execution work
- #5819 — lightweight PPL proxies for AA-measured competencies; complementary to this generative checkpoint suite
- #7090 — broader new-evals wish-list, including scalable proxies for several AA components

- Use no direct AA-II components. Every selected proxy must have an eval-only manifest and be excluded from Marin training data.
- A component score cannot depend solely on an LLM judge. Each selected benchmark must have a deterministic verifier or a gold answer.
- CC BY-NC datasets are acceptable, although none remain in the current shortlist.

| AA capability proxied | Selected eval | Source | License | Metric |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GDPval professional work | IFBench | [allenai/IFBench_test](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/IFBench_test) | ODC-BY 1.0 | Deterministic prompt-level constraint accuracy |
| GDPval professional work; SciCode | DS-1000 | [xlangai/DS-1000](https://huggingface.co/datasets/xlangai/DS-1000) | CC BY-SA 4.0 | Unit-test pass@1 |
| τ³-Banking | τ²-Bench-Verified Retail | [amazon-agi/tau2-bench-verified](https://github.com/amazon-agi/tau2-bench-verified) | MIT | Deterministic task success from state/action checks |
| Terminal-Bench | OpenThoughts-TBLite | [open-thoughts/OpenThoughts-TBLite](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-thoughts/OpenThoughts-TBLite) | Apache 2.0 | Container-test pass@1 |
| SciCode | CruxEval | [facebookresearch/cruxeval](https://github.com/facebookresearch/cruxeval) | MIT | Execution pass@1 for input/output prediction |
| HLE breadth | MMLU-Pro non-science categories | [TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro) | MIT | Gold multiple-choice accuracy |
| HLE hard math tail | OlympiadBench Math, English text-only open-ended subset | [OpenBMB/OlympiadBench](https://github.com/OpenBMB/OlympiadBench) | MIT in GitHub; Apache 2.0 in Hugging Face metadata | Exact, numeric, or symbolic answer accuracy |
| GPQA scientific reasoning | MMLU-Pro biology, chemistry, and physics categories | [TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro](https://huggingface.co/datasets/TIGER-Lab/MMLU-Pro) | MIT | Gold multiple-choice accuracy |
| CritPt physics | OlympiadBench Physics, English text-only open-ended subset | [OpenBMB/OlympiadBench](https://github.com/OpenBMB/OlympiadBench) | MIT in GitHub; Apache 2.0 in Hugging Face metadata | Exact, numeric, or symbolic answer accuracy |
| Omniscience | SimpleQA | [OpenAI simple-evals](https://github.com/openai/simple-evals) | MIT | Deterministic normalized gold match with correct `+1`, abstain `0`, incorrect `-1`; reference-answer conditional loss/PPL for base checkpoints |
| Long-context reasoning | MRCR | [openai/mrcr](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr) | MIT | Deterministic gold-answer similarity by context length and needle count |

FinanceBench, TriviaQA, BFCL, GPQA Diamond, and direct AA datasets are out of scope. MMLU-Pro is partitioned so the HLE and GPQA proxies do not score the same questions twice. Reference-answer conditional loss/PPL is an auxiliary base-checkpoint metric; generated-answer accuracy remains the post-training metric.

The first definition-of-done item remains open until the exact dataset and harness revisions, splits, and OlympiadBench configurations are pinned.

issues.author: ahmeda14960
issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tests whether DPO on IFBench-style preference data improves instruction following without overfitting to IFBench or damaging IFEval. The first completed Tulu-3 8B DPO runs built the shared IFBench/IFEval evaluation path, trained strict/loose/soft preference arms, and found a real positive signal: all DPO arms improved IFBench_test strict pass-all over the Tulu base, with the loose arm best on IFBench (+9.33 percentage points strict), while IFEval stayed flat-to-up. The issue is still open because the stronger paper-style full-train strict dataset and LR sweep were launched next, but no later result has been recorded in the issue. Current recommendation: treat IFBench-targeted DPO as promising on Tulu, but do not conclude the full recipe until the full-coverage LR sweep results are added.

### Helpful links
- Initial Tulu DPO result: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5244#issuecomment-2846928782
- W&B project: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/ifbench_dpo
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

DPO against a narrow instruction-following spec may improve benchmark compliance while degrading broader instruction following. This project tracks whether IFBench-targeted DPO actually preserves or improves instruction-following behavior when evaluated on both IFEval and IFBench.

IFEval is the continuity baseline. IFBench is the primary target because it is the broader, more adversarial instruction-following benchmark for this work. We should compare base instruct models, external DPO models, and our DPO checkpoints under the same generation and scoring harness.

## Hypothesis or Goal

North star: improve IFBench and IFEval without creating a model that only overfits the IFBench verifier/spec.

Initial goals:

- Train DPO on preference pairs derived from IFBench-style pass/fail signals.
- Evaluate every candidate on both IFEval and IFBench with consistent chat templates, stop tokens, and generation config.
- Track whether DPO gains are isolated to IFBench or transfer to IFEval.
- Test whether mixing SFT data with DPO data regularizes the model toward general instruction following while retaining IFBench gains.

### Links

- Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/dpo_sft_codex.md`
- Shared project notes: `.agents/projects/dpo_sft.md`
- W&B project: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/ifbench_dpo

## Results

Pending. Current runs include Tulu-3 8B DPO baselines and learning-rate sweeps on the paper-strict IFBench preference dataset.

comments.author: ahmeda14960
comments.body:
🤖 Update: initial Tülu DPO signal

- Built the eval path for the two target benchmarks: IFBench_test (300 OOD prompts) and Google IFEval (541 prompts), using the vendored IFBench/IFEvalG verifier stack and the shared scoring harness.
- Added and cached `allenai/Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-8B-DPO` revision `a7beb67`, then used it as the base for Tülu-side DPO experiments.
- Trained three first-pass Tülu DPO arms over IFBench-derived preference data: `strict`, `loose`, and `soft`. The Tülu vocab/export mismatch was fixed with `resize_vocab_to_match_tokenizer=True`, and all three arms completed/exported.
- Evaluated Tülu base + DPO arms on both IFBench_test and IFEval. Early sign: DPO improves IFBench without obvious IFEval damage.

Key result:

```text
Model             IFBench strict   IFBench loose   IFEval strict   IFEval loose
Tülu base              20.00%          26.00%          76.52%         79.67%
+DPO strict            25.00%          28.67%          80.04%         82.44%
+DPO loose             29.33%          33.67%          78.93%         83.55%
+DPO soft              27.00%          30.67%          77.08%         80.78%
```

Initial read: the IFBench-targeted DPO signal is real on Tülu. All three DPO arms beat the base on IFBench_test strict pass-all; `loose` is the best OOD IFBench arm at +9.33pp strict over base. IFEval also stays flat-to-up, with `strict` best on IFEval strict and `loose` best on IFEval loose.

Current next step: we built the paper-style full-train strict dataset from Gemini-vs-Llama-8B rollouts, filtered to max length 4096 (`24,153` pairs), tokenized it region-agnostically in us-central1/east5, and launched a one-epoch Tülu LR sweep (`3e-6`, `5e-6`, `2e-5`) on v5p-8 in us-east5. These runs test whether the stronger full-coverage dataset can improve the IFBench lift while preserving IFEval.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
On TPU, Snowball Step12 assigns different next-token log probabilities than H100 from token position 2048 onward. Up to position 2047 the two platforms agree to within TPU run-to-run noise. Step12 uses `sliding_window = 2048` with `global_every = 4`, so three of every four attention layers attend only to the last 2048 tokens. The divergence starts at that window size.

Impact: MATH500 on the same model, revision and Evalchemy commit scores 0.944 and 0.950 on H100 and 0.878, 0.882 (v6e-8, TP8) and 0.884 (v5p-8, TP4) on TPU. 39 items are correct on both H100 runs and wrong on TPU; 22 of them are long answers that drift to a different question.

Measurement: teacher-forced log probabilities of the same 10 texts on each platform (rendered Step12 chat prefix plus an H100-generated, H100-correct MATH500 completion; vLLM `/v1/completions` with `echo`, `logprobs=1`, `max_tokens=0`, concurrency 1). 35,801 scored positions; token ids are identical on both platforms.

| Positions | H100 vs TPU mean \|Δlogprob\| | top-1 token differs | TPU concurrency 1 vs 10 mean \|Δlogprob\| |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–2047 | 0.010–0.019 | 0.8–1.0% | 0.012–0.015 |
| 2048–2111 | 0.026 | 1.6% | – |
| 2368–2559 | 0.066 | 3.1–3.3% | – |
| 2048–3071 | 0.063 | 3.6% | 0.014 |
| 3072–4095 | 0.142 | 6.8% | 0.018 |

Pooled over all positions: mean \|Δ\| 0.056 (TPU self-noise 0.014), maximum 12.3 (TPU self-noise 1.1), top-1 differs at 2.8% of positions (TPU self-noise 0.86%). TPU's mean per-token negative log likelihood is higher on all 10 items.

The per-element window mask agrees across the three stacks. Each keeps the last W tokens including the query token:
- training: [`levanter/grug/attention/_core.py` L126](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8e99858a17df0463daac6b104f5eddb0ffa79ffd/lib/levanter/src/levanter/grug/attention/_core.py#L123-L126), `k >= q - (W - 1)`;
- H100 vLLM fork: [`grugmoe.py` L957-L964](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/01911be34fac8715347962a8d791ca34a879e01e/vllm/model_executor/models/grugmoe.py#L957-L964) passes `per_layer_sliding_window=2048` on local layers;
- TPU: [`grugmoe.py` L786](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py#L776-L787) passes the window as `attention_chunk_size`, which [`attention_interface.py` L496](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/layers/common/attention_interface.py#L494-L498) forwards as `sliding_window`; the RPA v3 kernel masks with [`q < k + W` at L494](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L493-L494).

The cause is not confirmed. Two unverified suspects on the TPU path:
- the RPA v3 sliding-window block skipping, which computes the first KV block to read from `kv_q_gap - sliding_window` ([kernel.py L388-L399](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L388-L399), [L916-L942](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L916-L942));
- KV-cache handling for the sliding-window layers.

Reproduce:
1. Serve `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02` at revision `50fe2f488aee7730bbccc721024b35229075602e`, bf16. TPU: v6e-8, TP8, tpu-inference `ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d`, vLLM `fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`. H100: H100x8, DP8 with expert parallelism, Marin vLLM fork build `01911be34fac`.
2. Run `python teacher_forced_logprobs.py --endpoint URL --model open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12-2026.10.02 --items teacher_forced_items.json --output DIR --concurrency 1` against each server. The client and items (sha256 `9d4779361b79259d36dcd2402d6fe686c81884d111cab550bb6c7fff158cdc4d`) are in `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/inputs/`.
3. Compare with `python compare_tf.py H100_DIR/results.json TPU_DIR/results.json` from the same folder, and bin `|Δlogprob|` by position.

Expected: TPU per-position log probabilities stay within TPU run-to-run noise of H100 at every position, including beyond 2048.

Next step: rerun the TPU side with `grugmoe_attention_mode` set to the dense reference path (`_dense_reference_attention` in `grugmoe.py`, which applies the window as an explicit mask). If dense-mode TPU matches H100 past position 2048, the defect is in the production RPA path.

Caveats: the H100 completions were re-tokenized from text because the eval record has no sampled token ids, and vLLM omits special tokens such as the leading `<|start_think|>` from returned text. Both platforms scored the same bytes, so the comparison is valid, but the first completion positions are not a replay of the original sampled trajectory.

Data:
- H100: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/teacher-h100x8/concurrency-1/`
- TPU v6e-8: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task236/teacher-v6e8/concurrency-{1,10}/`
- H100 MATH500 per-item and three-way tables: `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task224-math500/`

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 Correction to the next step in the description: a config-only dense-mode rerun is not available on the serving path.

- The served vLLM build (`fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`) never reads `grugmoe_attention_mode`; its Grug model always uses the `Attention` layer (`vllm/model_executor/models/grugmoe.py` L958-L964). Passing the field through `hf_overrides` changes nothing.
- The dense switch exists only in tpu-inference's reference JAX model ([`tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py` L233, L738-L804](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py#L738-L804)). That class is not in the JAX model registry used for serving, and its dense path ignores the KV cache.

The replacement control is a kernel-level test: run tpu-inference's ragged paged attention tests with Step12's shapes (sliding window 2048, page size 16, 32 query / 8 KV heads after padding) against the reference implementation on a v6e-4.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The 2048-token onset implicates local attention, but matching elementwise mask inequalities do not establish that TPU RPA visits the right KV blocks or reads intact cache pages. `GrugMoeAttention.__call__()` selects a dense path that computes from the full input without updating KV cache, or a production path that calls RPA v3. The measured TPU revision is the head of [tpu-inference#27](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/pull/27); [marin#9400](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9400) qualifies a June checkpoint, not Step12.

**Relevant code**
- [`grugmoe.py#L738-L805`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/models/jax/grugmoe.py#L738-L805) — dense and production attention paths
- [`attention_interface.py#L493-L510`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/layers/common/attention_interface.py#L493-L510) — window forwarded to RPA
- [`kernel.py#L388-L399`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L388-L399) — first KV block selection
- [`kernel.py#L493-L494`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L493-L494) — elementwise window mask
- [`kernel.py#L916-L942`](https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/blob/ae387b8bb7a644bbe7e17a9ce11bd701a012aa8d/tpu_inference/kernels/ragged_paged_attention/v3/kernel.py#L916-L942) — per-query-block traversal

# Proposed Fix

`GrugMoeAttention.__call__()` → `shared_attention()` → RPA v3 is the production call chain. The failing step within that chain is not established, so use the frozen Step12 inputs to isolate it:

1. Replay the issue's 10 teacher-forced inputs on the reported TPU revisions with `grugmoe_attention_mode=dense` and `production`; force one complete prefill per request because dense has no historical KV-cache reads, verify identical token IDs, and compare bins around position 2048 with the existing H100 results.
2. If dense agrees with H100, compare RPA v3 with a dense QKV reference at positions 2047, 2048, 2111, and 3072 across page and query-block boundaries, including full prefill, chunked prefill, decode, skipped KV blocks, and cache/page-table contents; otherwise find the first divergent layer output and compare its Q/K/V, RoPE, mask, and loaded weights with Levanter.
3. Fix the identified TPU fork path, add a regression across position 2048, rerun the frozen log-probability comparison and repeated MATH500 on the same checkpoint, and coordinate with the open `tpu-inference#27` stack before updating Marin's paired fork pin; the post-window H100–TPU error should return to measured TPU run-to-run noise before hardware qualification.

issues.body:
Every Iris job that requests a GPU extra gets `NCCL_DEBUG=INFO` with `NCCL_DEBUG_SUBSYS=INIT,BOOTSTRAP,ENV,NET,GRAPH,TUNING,RAS` from the default environment in `lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/types.py:779`. Marin's training launcher sets `NCCL_DEBUG` to `WARN` only when nothing is preset (`lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:418`, `setdefault`), so the Iris default wins for every training job.

On 2026-10-17 four 32-GPU SFT jobs (`/karan/task203-lr*`, cw-rno2a) emitted about 80,000 log lines per second, mostly `NCCL INFO` per-collective output, while log forwarding accepts about 34,500 lines per second; the hub fell about 90 minutes behind on that cluster's logs.

Reproduce: submit any GPU job without setting `NCCL_DEBUG` and read its task log; `NCCL INFO AllReduce: ... Algo TREE proto LL ...` lines appear for every collective.

Expected: GPU jobs default to `NCCL_DEBUG=WARN` (abort and transport errors remain visible), with INFO and the subsystem list set only by jobs that are debugging NCCL (for example the recovery or wedge repro experiments, which already set INFO explicitly).

Done when: the Iris GPU default is `WARN` without a subsystem list, Marin's training launcher no longer needs to guess, and the two call sites that want INFO set it themselves.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Design stage, 2026-10-16. We compare five supervised fine-tuning (SFT) mechanisms for agentic coding on one base, one task pool, one teacher and one supervised-token budget: plain SFT (one accepted demonstration per task), rejection-sampled SFT with resampling across epochs, relay SFT (#10027), recovery SFT, and plateau dropping (#10028). The earlier transfer experiments (#9920, #9984) compared plain SFT, rejection-sampled SFT, on-policy distillation and weight merging on non-agentic tasks; this experiment moves to agentic tasks under the eval policy (#10197) and drops merging and distillation. Nothing has trained yet except a learning-rate sweep of the control, which is in progress.

## Question

Which mechanism, if any, improves Snowball v0 on SWE-bench Verified and the terminal benchmarks over plain SFT at equal supervised tokens, without losing retention on GSM8K, BFCL-Parity and GPQA-Diamond.

## Fixed choices

- Base: Snowball v0 = `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Merge-Campaign3-DARE-Linear-02-2026.10.12` @ `4eeb756b`. v0 carries a diluted DARE graft of the allkimi relay SFT, so relay's lift reads smaller than it would on a pre-graft checkpoint; this is accepted because the question is what improves the release.
- Task pool: about 2,200 TMax environments (`allenai/TMax-SFT-16.5K`, tasks.zip) and about 2,100 SWE-smith tasks sampled from the Harbor packages in `DCAgent/swesmith-sandboxes-with_tests-oracle_verified_120s`, stratified by repository, SWE-bench Verified repositories removed, decontaminated through DataKit against SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and TBLite 2.0. Selection is outcome-blind. SWE-smith packages receive a git-history strip before the agent phase (#10212).
- Harness per task family, matching the policy's scoring agent: TMax under Terminus-2, SWE-smith under mini-swe-agent 2.1.0, both in Harbor under the policy pins.
- Teacher: GLM 5.3 through the internal inference service, 8 attempts per task, verified by each task's tests. v0 is never sampled except in relay, where it starts each task and GLM continues after a trigger (format error, context budget, completion claim).
- Recipe, shared by every arm: the #9984 comparison-arm settings (AdamW, betas 0.9/0.999, weight decay 0, clip 1.0, router bias frozen, batch 16 at 32k context, constant learning rate, loss averaged over supervised tokens), 3 epochs, replay of general SFT data (`nemotron_sft_v3`, reasoning kept) at one quarter of the agentic budget. The learning rate comes from the sweep below.

## Arms and token matching

B is the supervised-token count of the plain arm: the first passing attempt per task with at least one pass, one trajectory per task. Every arm trains on B agentic tokens plus the same replay slice for the same number of optimizer steps.

- Plain SFT (control): as above.
- RS-multi: identical task slots to plain; when a task recurs in a later epoch, a different passing attempt is used. Measures demonstration diversity at a fixed budget.
- Relay (#10027): v0's own turns stay in context with no loss; GLM's turns are trained; passing episodes subsampled to B. Episodes with no teacher turn are dropped.
- Recovery (phase 2): the plain trajectories; 20% receive one or two synthetic failed turns re-rendered in v0's measured error styles plus the real harness error, inserted through the parser; injections carry no loss, so the budget equals B by construction. Waits on a validated injection generator.
- Plateau dropping (#10028, phase 2): the plain trajectories; tokens whose loss has plateaued lose gradient; matched on optimizer steps, with gradient-carrying tokens reported. Waits on the trainer.

Phase 1 is plain, RS-multi and relay.

## Evaluation

Every arm, including plain, runs the retention gate (GSM8K, BFCL-Parity, GPQA-Diamond) and the agentic endpoint (SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.1, TBLite 2.0) under the policy's trial counts and pins. An arm passes when it has no decisive loss against plain on the gate and a decisive win over plain on at least one agentic benchmark with no decisive loss on the others, where decisive is the policy's rule (gap above 1.96 times the combined task-level standard error, each scaled by 1/sqrt(0.9)). One policy run resolves gaps of roughly 4 to 5 points on SWE-bench Verified and 8 to 10 on the terminal benchmarks; unresolved arms are reported with intervals and not promoted. Passing arms, plain and v0 go to the 23-benchmark tournament.

## Learning-rate sweep of the control

Running now, on pilot data (existing Qwen3.6-27B TMax traces and Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith traces, history-reading trials removed), four runs from v0 at 3e-7, 1e-6, 3e-6 and 1e-5, 3 epochs, recipe otherwise fixed. Screens per run: held-out validation loss on 5% of tasks, GSM8K, BFCL-Parity, SWE-bench Verified random-100 and a 100-task TBLite subset. Decision rule, fixed in advance: among rates with no decisive retention loss against v0, the best equal-weight mean of the two agentic screens; ties to the smaller rate. The chosen rate is confirmed once on the real plain-arm data and then frozen for all arms.

## Budget

Core (sweep, generation, phase 1, tournament) about 3,700 to 4,000 H100-hours; phase 2 adds about 2,400, of which 1,700 is an optional 20-epoch plateau comparison. GLM generation runs on the internal service and sandbox CPU and is outside the GPU budget.

## Status and next steps

- Pilot dataset and learning-rate sweep: in progress.
- Task pool, decontamination and package fix: in progress.
- Harness bring-up, one-task dry runs, a 200-task-per-family pass-rate pilot and a relay dry run: in progress. The full 8-attempt generation waits on their results.
- Then: phase-1 training, first-stage evaluation, tournament for passers; phase 2 when its code exists.

Design notes and diagrams are kept in the maintainer's notes and will be attached as results land.

## Decision log

- 2026-10-15: scope cut to SFT only; merging and on-policy distillation dropped. Base set to Snowball v0.
- 2026-10-16: one harness per task family following the policy's scoring agents; GLM 5.3 as the single teacher with regenerated traces instead of reusing Kimi and Qwen traces; RS arm redefined as resampling across epochs after the token-budgeted variant was found to re-weight tasks; task eligibility defined by teacher success only; unfiltered-SFT control dropped; primary endpoint set to the agentic benchmarks with the tournament secondary; git-history leak found in the SWE-smith packages and a strip added to the pool build.

🤖 Teacher generation bring-up: one-task dry runs

## TL;DR

GLM 5.3 now runs end to end in both harnesses (Harbor `016dd78b`, Daytona sandboxes, run from cw-us-east-02a):
- TMax under Terminus-2, with the 65,536 / 16,384 limits from the policy;
- SWE-smith under the mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 adapter, with a 32,768-token window.

**The adapter question is answered.** The mini-swe-agent adapter runs a raw SWE-smith Harbor package unchanged, and the dry-run trace fit inside 32k (largest prompt 13.4k tokens). One trace says nothing about the length distribution; the pilot will measure it.

**The GLM pass on SWE-smith read the fix from git history** (#10212). Before the SWE-smith pass-rate pilot, the packages need the history-stripped repair.

**The pilot has not started.** It waits on a capacity confirmation for the GLM service.

## Per trial

| | TMax `task_000000_5c5b0938` | SWE-smith `swesmith-00003` |
|---|---|---|
| Reward | 0 in the first run, 1 in a rerun | 1 in both runs |
| Model calls | 4 | 16 to 17 |
| Prompt tokens (total / largest) | 9.3k to 10.1k / 3.7k | 145k to 156k (about 93% prefix-cached) / 13.4k |
| Completion tokens (reasoning) | 5.1k to 6.2k (4.2k to 5.2k) | 3.4k to 3.6k (0.5k to 0.8k) |
| Model time | 39 s | 16 s |
| Trial wall time | 42 to 93 s (environment build 3 to 45 s) | 74 to 80 s (verifier 20 to 25 s) |

## Effective generation settings

Both clients send only `model` and `max_tokens=16384`, so GLM runs on the service defaults. GLM 5.3's template then renders `Reasoning Effort: Max`.

Every request is logged by an in-cluster proxy. The log records the settings as sent and the full reply, reasoning included. The proxy also serves `/tokenize` with the `zai-org/GLM-5.3` tokenizer, because the mini-swe-agent context limiter needs it and the relay does not provide it. Its token counts matched the service on every request.

## Transcripts

Both harnesses write Harbor ATIF trajectories:
- **Terminus-2:** each step's message is the JSON action, and the reasoning is in `reasoning_content`.
- **mini-swe-agent:** native `bash` tool calls with `{returncode, output}` observations, but the trajectory **drops GLM's reasoning**. Training rows are therefore rebuilt from the proxy log, which keeps it. That rebuild checks clean on both dry runs.

## What the agent can see

Measured with an oracle-agent probe during the agent phase:

| | TMax (converted) | SWE-smith (raw package) |
|---|---|---|
| `/tests` | absent | absent |
| `/solution` | absent | absent |
| Other task files | none | none |
| Git history | no repository | 944 branches, including `main` and the full history |

The SWE-smith dry-run pass used that history: it ran `git show 614b134:<file>`, then checked its edit against that file. Details are in #10212.

## Other findings

- **TMax is not in Harbor format** in `tasks.zip`. The pool converts it with TMax's own `convert_to_harbor.py` at `hamishivi/tmax@6d3d606c`, minus 181 environments with hidden verifier assets, giving 2,019 tasks.
- **The dry-run TMax task looks flawed.** It runs an OpenMP parallel loop over the outer LU loop with 4 threads, while the test expects the sequential determinant. The task failed once and passed once.

## Next

- **TMax pilot:** 200 tasks x 2 attempts, seed 20261016, drawn uniformly from 1,963 eligible tasks (the pool minus #202's held-out ids). Staged; starts when capacity is confirmed.
- **SWE-smith pilot:** 200 x 2, stratified by repository, on the history-stripped packages.
- **Relay dry run:** 20 tasks per family, with v0 served by the policy serving config. GLM takes over on these triggers:
  - format error: GLM writes one repair turn;
  - context budget at 0.75 of the window: GLM continues to the end;
  - completion claim: v0's reply is withheld and logged, and GLM continues to the end.

Run folders: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/sft-shootout/generation/dryrun/{tmax-dry1,tmax-dry2,swe-dry3,swe-dry4,visibility1}`

comments.body:
🤖 TMax pass-rate pilot with GLM 5.3 under Terminus-2: pass@1 0.77, pass@2 0.83 on 200 tasks × 2.

**TL;DR:** GLM 5.3 solves most TMax tasks. Only 1% of trials ended with no reward. The median trajectory is 9.6k tokens, but 12.8% of conversations exceed 32k. 9 of 400 trials (2.25%) went through context summarization, and those cannot become single 32k training rows.

**Setup**
- Tasks: 200 drawn uniformly (seed 20261016) from TMax pool P (#206): 1,918 eligible tasks after all 101 held-out ids were removed.
- Packages: `tmax-packages.parquet` (`allenai/TMax-SFT-16.5K@848e2182` converted with `hamishivi/tmax@6d3d606c`).
- Agent: Terminus-2 at the eval-policy Harbor pin (`marin-community/harbor@016dd78b`), 65,536 input / 16,384 output tokens, agent timeout 1,800 s, Daytona sandboxes.
- Model: GLM 5.3 through the bulk service. Clients send only `model` and `max_tokens=16384`, so the service defaults apply and the chat template renders "Reasoning Effort: Max".
- Concurrency 32. The run took 66 min of wall time (00:19–01:25 UTC).

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Trials | 400 (200 tasks × 2), 0 Harbor retries |
| pass@1 (all trials / graded only) | 0.7725 / 0.7803 |
| pass@2 | 0.825 |
| No reward (infra or agent error before grading) | 4 trials (1.0%): TmuxBatchProtocolError 2, TmuxSessionEndedError 2 |
| Agent timeouts (1,800 s; still graded) | 9 |
| Trial wall time, median / p90 / max | 100 s / 342 s / 1,924 s |
| Model calls per trial, median / p90 / max | 6 / 11 / 61 |
| Sequence length per conversation (last prompt + completion), median / p90 / max | 9,596 / 50,709 / 65,453 tokens |
| Conversations over 32,768 tokens | 12.8% |
| Assistant tokens per trial (reasoning included), median / p90 / max | 9,910 / 33,905 / 239,616 |
| Reasoning tokens per trial, median / p90 / max | 7,101 / 28,433 / 194,281 |
| Trials with context summarization | 9 (2.25%) |

comments.body:
🤖 Relay rounds broken by a preempted student server ([#10237](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10237)).

**Affected rounds**
- TMax relay shard-02 round 1: 198 of 200 trials errored, 14:33-15:13 UTC on 2026-10-17. Moved to `traces/tmax-relay/shard-02/round-1.failed-0a6b03ad`; it will be rerun. It was never published.
- SWE-smith relay shard-00 round 3: 85 of 97 trials errored, from about 08:29 UTC. Its 32 valid rows are published; trials that raised without a GLM reply don't count as relay runs.

I'm checking every other round for a student preemption and will post the full list.

**Cause.** In relay mode, the v0 student runs as a child inference job. When that job was preempted, Iris rescheduled it on another host. The relay proxy kept calling the address resolved once at startup (`lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py:682`). Every student call then failed with `httpx.ConnectError`, the agents got HTTP 500, and Harbor still exited 0.

**Fix** (`task/212` @ [`174906474a`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/174906474a8039d1ff8989e8f6d53103242cfec1)):
- On a connection error, the proxy looks up the student's current address and retries for up to 20 minutes.
- The proxy logs its own failures, which used to go unlogged.
- A run fails, with no `_SUCCESS`, when more than 20% of its trials raise without a reply.

The relay lanes are being resubmitted on this commit.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
Since 2026-10-18 05:49 UTC, every mini-swe-agent trial on Harbor main fails before its first model call, and SWE-bench Verified scores read 0. Marin main pins Harbor `18e71265`, so any SWE eval launched from marin main today is affected. Harbor `38742b0f` on `benfeuer/eval-campaign-09-25-runtime` has the fix, but Harbor main does not.

Harbor installs the agent inside each sandbox with `uv tool install mini-swe-agent==2.1.0` ([`mini_swe_agent.py` L456 on main](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/blob/18e712655917ee1c5f82624809339daff3a26a9e/src/harbor/agents/installed/mini_swe_agent.py#L456)). mini-swe-agent 2.1.0 requires only `litellm>=1.75.5`. litellm 1.106.0, released at 05:49 UTC, raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp'` on the first query.

Symptom: the vLLM server logs `/tokenize` requests but no `/v1/chat/completions`. Each trajectory has 2 steps and 0 prompt/completion tokens. The orchestrator log does not show the import error, because the captured agent stdout is cut off before it. The shootout's plain-arm SWE r100 screen read 0/99: 98 trials ended in `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError`, 1 in `VerifierRuntimeError`, 1 in `AgentTimeoutError`.

Local repro, against any OpenAI-compatible server set in `HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE`:

```python
# uv run --no-project --with mini-swe-agent==2.1.0 --with litellm==1.106.0 repro.py
from minisweagent.models.litellm_model import LitellmModel
LitellmModel(model_name="hosted_vllm/m", model_kwargs={"api_key": "EMPTY"}).query(
    [{"role": "system", "content": "s"}, {"role": "user", "content": "u"}]
)
```

It raises `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'mcp'` and sends no request. With `litellm==1.103.5` the request goes through. With Harbor 38742b0f's install (`uv tool install mini-swe-agent==2.1.0 --with mcp==2.3.0`) it also goes through: litellm 1.106.0 + mcp 2.3.0.

Who is affected: every mini-swe-agent eval and SWE-smith generation trial whose sandbox installed after 05:49 UTC on 2026-10-18, on Harbor `016dd78b` (the September campaign pin) or `18e71265` (marin main). Terminus-2 (TBLite, TB2), Evalchemy and BFCL do not install mini-swe-agent and are unaffected. The task204 LR-sweep SWE screens finished before 05:49 UTC and are valid.

Fix options:
1. Recommended: port 38742b0f's install change (`--with mcp==2.3.0` plus the setup-time import check) to Harbor main, then advance marin's Harbor pin. The setup check turns this kind of dependency drift into a setup failure, not a 0 score. Runs on the fix use litellm 1.106.0 instead of the earlier < 1.106 client, so comparisons should rerun their baseline under the same install.
2. Add `--exclude-newer 2026-10-18T05:00:00Z` to the install. This reproduces the pre-incident dependency set exactly, but the date must be bumped by hand later.
3. Pin `litellm<1.106` in the install. This is narrower, but leaves the other mini-swe-agent dependencies unpinned.

The shootout reruns its SWE screens (three arms plus v0) on 38742b0f. Shootout: #10213. Eval policy: #10197.


Incident note: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/789

spillover_issues.author: wmoss
spillover_issues.body:
#### **Context & Goal**
Currently, `smallquery` stands up a transient Ballista scheduler and executor pool on-demand per step, introducing a ~1-minute Kubernetes pod scheduling delay and requiring ad-hoc cluster lifecycle management inside python pipeline steps. 

To provide instant query submission for interactive queries, we want to stand up a persistent, long-running Ballista cluster on Iris with a non-preemptible scheduler and a baseline warm pool of preemptible, low-priority executors.

---

#### **Proposed Architecture**

1. **Non-Preemptible Scheduler (24/7)**:
   * Run a lightweight, non-preemptible Ballista Scheduler task (`cpu=0.5, memory="1Gi"`) on Iris with a stable service endpoint.
   * Running 24/7 incurs negligible cost (~$10/month) while guaranteeing that query DAGs and state are never lost due to node eviction.

2. **Preemptible & Low-Priority Executor Pool with Baseline Warmth**:
   * Maintain a baseline warm pool of **2–5 preemptible (Spot) executor workers** running continuously for instant query execution on small queries.
   * **Low Iris Priority**: Configure baseline warm workers with low Iris job priority so Iris can automatically preempt them to yield cluster capacity whenever higher-priority jobs (e.g., training, ferries) require resources.
   * Support dynamic bursting to **80–100 preemptible workers** when large batch pipeline stages are submitted.
   * Schedulers handle worker evictions mid-query by automatically re-assigning lost task partitions to remaining workers.

3. **Idle Scale-Down**:
   * Burst workers scale back down to the baseline warm pool (2–5 workers) after an idle timeout (e.g., 10–15 minutes of query inactivity).

---

#### **Key Requirements & Implementation Tasks**

* [ ] **Deployment Config**: Add launcher manifest / script to register the long-running Ballista Scheduler on Iris with non-preemptible resource constraints.
* [ ] **Preemptible & Low-Priority Provisioning**: Configure baseline warm executor task specs with preemptible constraints (`max_retries_preemption=10`) and low Iris job priority so Iris can preempt them for higher-priority work.
* [ ] **Baseline & Burst Management**: Update `smallquery.deploy` / client launcher to target the stable scheduler endpoint and scale the executor pool dynamically between baseline warmth and peak stage requirements.
* [ ] **Idle TTL Scaling**: Implement an idle timeout worker reaper that returns the executor pool to baseline size when no queries are active.

## Description

Levanter still has no in-framework rank-level straggler detection: the trainer logs end-to-end step time but never attributes which rank/host is chronically slow. This was specced in #4235 / #4236 and fully implemented twice — #4240 (host-side, `multihost_broadcast_sync`) and #4241 (JAX distributed KV store), both with tests — but both PRs were closed unmerged (2026-04-28) and the issue auto-closed for inactivity (2026-06-28), not on the merits. `StragglerReporter` is absent from `main` today.

The need is live and recurring:

- The team just merged a **reactive** NCCL collective-hang watchdog (#7350) after a GB200 run silently wedged with all ranks frozen together (#7344). A lagging rank is exactly what straggler reporting surfaces *before* it becomes a wedge — this is the proactive complement to that watchdog.
- Slow-process pathologies keep costing debug time with no per-rank attribution: slow-loader stalls (#7039), prefetch-queue starvation (#7474), and per-host RAM-leak OOMs where engineers hand-rolled per-rank telemetry (#6774, #6908).
- Recent MFU work computes slowest/p50 step time manually per config (#7279, #7201, #7012, #7052); Iris tracks degraded nodes at the cluster level (#2827) but nothing does it inside the training loop.

Rebase #4240 as the starting point (preferred over #4241 — host-side, no KV-store dependency).

### Definition of Done

- A trainer callback logs per-rank step duration to the standard tracker (no profiler trace required), reporting min/median/max + top-k slowest ranks with rolling/EWMA history to separate one-off stalls from chronic lag.
- Cheap enough to leave enabled at moderate cadence during pretraining.
- Focused tests for the aggregation/reporting logic.
- As a byproduct, exposes the slowest-process step time needed for a valid aggregate-throughput denominator.

spillover_issues.body:
# Floppy Phoenix schedules for December (and maybe January)

Building on @ClassicLarry et al. candidate work in [the GB200 TPS tracker (#7201)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7201), I've been Rick Rubin-ing on [Floppy Phoenix](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html) to see how post-training changes model choice under a few different timelines that @ihodes was curious about at our last hero run meeting.

Under the very heavily asterisked assumptions below, d6144 4-of-128 seems about right so not actually a huge prior update here. One thing I'd raise is that (if we want a more pretrained model that we think can support longer RL runs) d7168 (or another larger model via sparsity or depth scaling) is worth benchmarking to see how much it tanks our MFU v.s helps our model size.

## TL;DR

My current recommendation is to plan around d6144 4-of-128. If December 24 is fixed, the unresolved choice is whether to hand off on November 15 or December 1. I would consider d7168 only for a January 15 release, and only if its measured pretraining and RL pace are close to the estimates here.

We are trying to ship a broadly useful model, roughly at the capability level tracked by the [Artificial Analysis index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/). Everything below assumes that pretraining starts August 15. The MFU estimates use Larry et al.'s measurements and the extrapolation formulas in #7201. RL is modeled as fully on-policy, so rollout generation and policy updates happen in sequence. I assume 15% downtime from operational issues, plus seven pretraining days for long-context extension and early cooldowns.

No row is measured end-to-end. The d6144 pretraining pace is projected from one rack, d7168 pace is forecast, and every RL figure is an unmeasured ceiling.

| post-training start | release | provisional model | pretraining tokens | illustrative RL response-token upper bound<sup>1</sup> | decision status |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| December 1 | December 24 | d6144 4-of-128 ([scenario inputs](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75)) | ≈20.8T | ≈0.5T | stretch; the upper bound reserves no time outside RL |
| November 15 | December 24 | d6144 4-of-128 ([scenario inputs](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=25000&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75)) | ≈17.4T | ≈0.9T | open trade: 3.3T pretraining tokens for 13.6 post-training days |
| December 1 | January 15 | d7168 4-of-128 ([unmeasured scenario](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.757)) | ≈14.5T | ≈0.8T | only if measured pace supports it; d6144 is the fallback |

<sup>1</sup> This spends the full effective post-training window on one synchronous RL loop. It reserves no time for SFT, evaluation, verifier work, recovery, safety work, or release packaging. We also have not decided whether "response tokens" means generated, accepted, or learner tokens.

All d6144 calculations use 20.0B active parameters. That convention is still unresolved in #7201.

## Why doesn't the fastest model win?

For a December 1 handoff, the fastest d5120 row gets 27.4T pretraining tokens versus 20.8T for d6144. The loss fit assigns a penalty to the smaller active model, even though it gets more pretraining tokens and can run more RL cycles.

[ScaleRL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13786) motivates a sigmoid in log RL compute. [Floppy Phoenix](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75) then assumes that the RL ceiling grows with model size. The [Nicholas Roberts et al. overtraining paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.01411) is another reason to include inference-time compute when sizing the pretrained model. None of these results calibrates final Marin capability.

Under those assumptions, d8192 has the lowest predicted reducible loss in all three schedules. I do not trust that result enough to train d8192: there are no d7168–d8192 throughput points, the loss fit has no prediction interval, and we do not have a Marin RL scaling curve. This is useful as sensitivity analysis, not as a model ranking. I would measure d7168 and d8192 to see where MFU falls off.

## The three schedules

### What if post-training starts December 1 and we release December 24?

This is tight: 19.6 effective post-training days. The [d6144 4-of-128 plan](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=13889&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75) gets about 20.8T pretraining tokens and an illustrative 0.5T RL response-token ceiling.

The [d5120 4-of-64 plan](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=8.8356) gets 27.4T pretraining tokens and a 0.8T RL ceiling. The current loss fit ranks it below d6144; we do not have a measured released-model quality comparison.

If its MFU holds up, [d6144 4-of-256](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=11111&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=35.35) gets about 16.7T pretraining tokens and a 0.4T RL ceiling. Its quality advantage over 4-of-128 is unmeasured, and the current fit assigns it none.

### What if pretraining ends November 15?

For [d6144](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.18e24&steps=25000&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75), the earlier handoff gives up about 3.3T pretraining tokens and adds 13.6 effective post-training days. We could use that time for more shots at goal on the recipe, or raise the illustrative ceiling from 0.5T to 0.9T response tokens.

The 0.9T figure is closer to the scale in the [MAI technical report](https://microsoft.ai/pdf/mai-thinking-1.pdf), but the comparison is pretty fuzzy. Their token accounting and post-training stages might not match ours.

We do not have much signal on shorter pretraining versus shorter post-training. The ongoing A2B run might give us some: if much lower pretraining loss does not make RL easier, maybe we should take the earlier handoff.

### What do we buy by waiting until January 15?

Releasing January 15 instead of December 24 adds 18.7 effective post-training days, 2.8e24 post-training hardware FLOPs, and 18% more total hardware compute.

[d7168](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=22222&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.757) gets about 14.5T pretraining tokens and has a 0.8T illustrative RL ceiling. I would only use it if measured training and RL pace make those two estimates credible. [d6144 is the fallback](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/floppy-phoenix/2026.07.24.3/index.html?fam=marin&C=3.74e24&steps=27778&tps=4000000&c_total_mult=17.75): 20.8T pretraining tokens and a 1.0T RL ceiling.

## What would be helpful to measure

- Define the RL token accounting, then run one complete synchronous RL cycle for each viable width. Report prompt, generated, accepted, and learner tokens; group size; response lengths; policy updates; and generation, update, synchronization, and total wall time.

- Measure d7168 and d8192 MFU with the same accounting as #7201. If d7168 is already falling off the throughput curve, use d6144 for every schedule.

- Cut another A2B cooldown so that Ben can run his existing post-training recipe on top of it. Knowing whether lower pretraining loss makes post-training easier in our setup would help us choose which phase to compress.

<details>
<summary>Full candidate table</summary>

| candidate | params, B (active / total) | TPS basis | 11-rack TPS | 11-rack 6NT utilization<sup>2</sup> | assumed RL cycle, seconds | pretraining tokens, T<sup>3</sup> | RL response-token ceiling, T<sup>4</sup> | modeled reducible-loss gap vs d8192<sup>5</sup> |
|---|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| d5120 4-of-64 | 14.6 / 129 | projected from 8 racks | 3.740M | 18.6% | 8.5 | 27.4 / 23.0 | 0.8 / 1.3 / 1.6 | 10.1% / 9.4% |
| d5120 4-of-128 | 14.5 / 250 | projected from 2 racks | 3.346M | 16.5% | 11.2 | 24.5 / 20.6 | 0.6 / 1.0 / 1.2 | 10.5% / 9.9% |
| d5120 8-of-256 EP | 14.5 / 249 | projected from 2 racks | 3.254M | 16.1% | 11.4 | 23.8 / 20.0 | 0.6 / 1.0 / 1.2 | 10.6% / 10.0% |
| d6144 4-of-128 <sup>C</sup> | 20.0 / 355 | projected from 1 rack | 2.833M | 19.3% | 13.2 | 20.8 / 17.4 | 0.5 / 0.9 / 1.0 | 5.5% / 5.0% |
| d6144 4-of-256 <sup>C</sup> | 20.0 / 707 | projected from 2 racks | 2.273M | 15.5% | 18.5 | 16.7 / 14.0 | 0.4 / 0.6 / 0.7 | 6.3% / 5.9% |
| d7168 4-of-128 <sup>E</sup> | 27.2 / 483 | MFU forecast | ≈1.974M | ≈18.3% | 16.5 | 14.5 / 12.1 | 0.4 / 0.7 / 0.8 | 2.1% / 1.9% |
| d7680 4-of-128 <sup>E</sup> | 31.3 / 555 | MFU forecast | ≈1.668M | ≈17.8% | 18.5 | 12.2 / 10.3 | 0.4 / 0.6 / 0.7 | 0.9% / 0.8% |
| d8192 4-of-128 <sup>E</sup> | 35.6 / 631 | MFU forecast | ≈1.434M | ≈17.4% | not estimated | 10.5 / 8.8 | not estimated | reference |

<sup>2</sup> `6NT utilization = 6 × active parameters × tokens per second / peak hardware FLOP/s`.

<sup>3</sup> December 1 / November 15 post-training starts.

<sup>4</sup> December 1→December 24 / November 15→December 24 / December 1→January 15. These are unmeasured ceilings from the assumed cycle times, not forecasts.

<sup>5</sup> Relative gap in the reducible part of the base-loss fit for December 1 / November 15. This is uncalibrated to released-model quality and has no prediction interval.

`C` marks the unresolved active-parameter convention. `E` marks a pace forecast with no measured throughput point.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Schedule math and assumptions</summary>

`hardware FLOPs = effective days × 86,400 × 704 × 2.5e15`

| pretraining start | post-training start | release | calendar days (pre / post) | effective days (pre / post) | peak hardware FLOPs (pre / post / total) |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| August 15 | December 1 | December 24 | 108 / 23 | 84.8 / 19.6 | 1.29e25 / 2.97e24 / 1.59e25 |
| August 15 | November 15 | December 24 | 92 / 39 | 71.2 / 33.2 | 1.08e25 / 5.04e24 / 1.59e25 |
| August 15 | December 1 | January 15 | 108 / 45 | 84.8 / 38.3 | 1.29e25 / 5.82e24 / 1.87e25 |

- Assume an average of 11 active NVL72 racks, 10–12 in practice, or 704 working GB200s for 1.76e18 peak BF16 FLOP/s.
- Effective pretraining days are `0.85 × calendar days − 7`; effective post-training days are `0.85 × calendar days`. The 7 pretraining days are 4 days for long context and 3 days for cooldown checkpoints.
- TPS projections come from #7201 and scale from 12 racks to our 11-rack average. d7168–d8192 use an MFU forecast.
- Useful pretraining FLOPs are `6 × active parameters × tokens`.
- The Floppy Phoenix links use compute normalized to its 20% reference MFU: 3.18e24 for the December 24 budget and 3.74e24 for the January 15 budget. This is not directly comparable to the peak hardware FLOPs above.
- The post-training calculation uses a 4M-response-token batch. Generation, policy update, and synchronization happen in sequence.
- The loss fit does not model a quality benefit from total expert count.

</details>
